title: Garlic Knots
subtitle: Tied pizza dough rolls tossed in garlic butter and parsley
excerpt: Garlic knots are strips of pizza dough tied into a knot, baked until puffed and golden, then tossed hot in a generous amount of garlic butter and parsley. They're an Italian-American pizzeria side dish and one of the best things to do with leftover pizza dough.
sourceNotes: Garlic knots are an Italian-American pizzeria invention, widely associated with New York pizza restaurants in the 1970s and 80s, traditionally made from leftover pizza dough scraps.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked and cooled knots. Reheat at 180°C for 8 minutes and toss with fresh garlic butter.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch from a double quantity of pizza dough: they keep for a day and reheat well.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Form and refrigerate the knots (before baking) for up to 12 hours. Bake from cold, adding two minutes to the cook time.

content.text: Garlic knots are strips of pizza dough tied into simple knots, baked until golden and puffed, then tossed immediately in butter, garlic, and parsley while still hot. The garlic butter soaks into the warm dough in the minute after tossing. They're quick, cheap, and better than any bread roll you'll make in the same amount of time.

Combine {{strong-bread-flour}}, {{yeast-fast-action}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}} in a bowl. Add {{olive-oil}} and {{water}} and mix to a dough. Knead for eight minutes until smooth and elastic. Cover and prove for one hour until doubled.
Heat the oven to 220°C (fan 200°C / gas mark 7). Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface. Roll it into a rectangle about 30 x 20 cm and cut into twelve strips, each roughly 2 cm wide.
Tie each strip into a simple overhand knot, tucking the ends underneath. Arrange on a lightly oiled baking tray with a little space between each knot.

Bake for 12 to 15 minutes until puffed and golden. While the knots bake, melt {{unsalted-butter}} in a small pan over medium heat. Add {{garlic}} and cook gently for one to two minutes until fragrant but not coloured. Remove from the heat and stir in {{parsley-flat}} and {{sea-salt-flakes}}.
Transfer the hot knots immediately to a large bowl. Pour the garlic butter over and toss to coat every knot. If using {{parmesan}}, add it now and toss again. Serve straight from the bowl.

items.symptom: The knots unravel in the oven
items.cause: Not tied tightly enough, or dough too relaxed.
items.fix: Tie the knot firmly and tuck both ends underneath: the weight holds the knot in place during baking. Rest the shaped knots for five minutes before baking.

items.symptom: The garlic burns before the butter is ready
items.fix: Melt the butter over medium-low heat and add the garlic when the butter is liquid but not bubbling. One to two minutes is enough: you want fragrant, not browned.

items.symptom: The knots are dense and doughy inside
items.cause: Under-proved dough, or oven not hot enough.
items.fix: Prove the dough until really doubled. The oven must be fully preheated to 220°C before the knots go in.

items.symptom: The butter runs off and pools on the tray
items.cause: Knots not hot enough, or too much butter.
items.fix: Toss the knots immediately out of the oven while they're still very hot. The warm dough absorbs the butter in seconds. Toss thoroughly.

content.text: Garlic knots are a New York pizzeria invention, reportedly created in the 1970s as a way to use up the trimmings of stretched pizza dough. They became a standard side at New York and New Jersey Italian-American restaurants and have since spread across American cooking. Make them with leftover pizza dough from the New York pizza recipe, or make the dough specifically for a batch of knots to serve with pasta or soup.
